media:group.media:description:

entry.title: Décoloniser les salons du livre d’art et l’éducation en design

media:group.media:title: Décoloniser les salons du livre d’art et l’éducation en design
media:group.media:description:
avec Pascale Obolo et Marly Jean-Noel & Victoria Owusu
Alors que le réseau international des salons du livre d’art ne cesse de s’étendre, quelles mesures organisationnelles et ambitieuses les salons peuvent-ils mettre en œuvre pour garantir la représentation des pays du Sud? Une discussion animée par Pascale Obolo, coauteure du guide pratique « Decolonizing Art Book Fairs » et fondatrice de l’African Art Book Fair ainsi que du magazine et laboratoire artistique et critique AFRIKADAA. En discussion avec Marly Jean-Noel, organisatrice en 2026 de l’exposition et conférence L’expérience noire en design et Victoria Owusu, designer créative spécialisée en identité visuelle et stratégie de contenu.

entry.title: Voices of Quebec | Les Voix du Québec

media:group.media:title: Voices of Quebec | Les Voix du Québec
media:group.media:description:
Join us for this student-led roundtable that offers an introduction to the linguistic landscape of Quebec and brings four language experts, each speaking to the space occupied by the four major language groups in Quebec, namely the French language, the English language, Indigenous languages (including revitalization) and finally, Heritage languages (spoken among immigrants in Quebec).
Rejoignez-nous pour cette table ronde animée par des étudiants qui propose une introduction au paysage linguistique du Québec et réunisse quatre experts en langues, qui s’expriment chacun sur la place occupée par les quatre principaux groupes linguistiques au Québec, à savoir la langue française, la langue anglaise, les langues autochtones (y compris leur revitalisation) et enfin, les langues d’origine (parlées par les immigrant·e·s au Québec).
Organized by: Isha Jain; Romain Chambon; Patrick Lewis With: Université de Montréal, Anthropology department
Organisé par: Isha Jain; Romain Chambon; Patrick Lewis Avec: Le Département d'Anthropologie de l'Université de Montréal

entry.title: National Day for Truth and Reconciliation: Confronting Our Past

media:group.media:title: National Day for Truth and Reconciliation: Confronting Our Past
media:group.media:description:
Join us as the Office of Indigenous Directions invites the university community to participate in a day of reflection and learning, following the publication of a long-awaited report, Exploring Concordia’s Colonial Past.
A panel discussion about the report on Concordia's colonial past and its contents is moderated by Peter Gossage (Distinguished Professor Emeritus, Dept. of History), with the participation of: • Colby Gaudet, the report's author and SSHRC Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of History at Dalhousie University • Kahérakwas Donna Goodleaf, Director, Decolonizing Curriculum and Pedagogy • Sigwan Thivierge, Associate Professor, First Peoples Studies & Linguistics • Lisa White, Executive Director, Equity Office
00:02 4th Space Intro 01:26 Opening remakrds Manon Tremblay 06:11 Panel Introduction 07:39 Exploring Concordia's Colonial Past, Presentation by Colby Gaudet 37:35 Panel Discussion 01:19:12 Q&A 01:57:36 Final Thoughts
About the report:
In 2021, Concordia commissioned then doctoral student Colby Gaudet to investigate the university’s historical foundations and produce a report that would help situate the university’s past within the wider context of colonialism and Indigenous experiences.
The research focused on the Grey Nuns, whose former motherhouse is part of Concordia’s campus, the founding institutions of Loyola College and Sir George Williams University and their respective connections to the Jesuits and the YMCA, all of which played roles in broader colonial systems in Canada.
By examining these histories, the report invites the Concordia community to reflect on the university’s past and to support ongoing efforts toward reconciliation and decolonization.
You can download the report here: https://www.concordia.ca/indigenous/resources/colonial-past.html

entry.title: Launch of Pathways to Impact with Prem Sooriyakumar and Brett Cox

media:group.media:title: Launch of Pathways to Impact with Prem Sooriyakumar and Brett Cox
media:group.media:description:
Join project team, Prem Sooriyakumar and Brett Cox, to learn more about the launch of Pathways to Impact!
Born from various sustainability lead and focused consultations regarding research impact, Concordia’s Office of the Vice President, Research Innovation and Impact (OVPRII) has launched a new web platform for its Pathways to Impact initiative, an ongoing collaboration with units from across the university designed to help researchers strengthen their research impact.
About the Speakers:
• Prem Sooriyakumar is Tamil, originally arrived as a refugee to Tiohtià:ke, from Jaffna, Sri Lanka. Currently a Senior Knowledge Broker at the OVPRII. He works with researchers on knowledge mobilization planning and research impact development and strategy. Additionally, Prem has been developing and supporting the institutional Pathways to Impact initiative and is one of the senior strategic advisors on the Abundant Intelligences NFRF-T research project, a majority Indigenous lead research project on Artificial Intelligences.
• Brett Cox is a third-generation settler originally from Brantford, Ontario – land that is situated on the traditional territory of the Neutral, Anishnawbe and Haudenosaunee peoples. Since June 2023, Brett has worked as Coordinator of Sustainability in Research at the OVPRII. His work involves coordinating various projects aimed at meeting the goals and strategies of the Sustainability in Research action plan. In addition to any questions related to the Pathways to Impact initiative, you can contact Brett for support with exploring sustainable research practices, developing a research impact plan, and any questions related to Concordia's Sustainability in Research action plan.

entry.title: Indigenizing and Decolonizing Sustainability Curriculum at Concordia

media:group.media:title: Indigenizing and Decolonizing Sustainability Curriculum at Concordia
media:group.media:description:
Join us for the next event as part of the Sustainability Action Plan 2026-30 Launch to celebrate Concordia's new sustainability roadmap.
Learn about the new opportunities and explore ongoing efforts to decolonize sustainability curriculum through partnerships with the Office of Decolonizing Curriculum and Pedagogy, with Donna Goodleaf, Director, Decolonizing and Indigenizing Curriculum and Pedagogy, and Rebecca Tittler, Academic Advisor and Administrative Coordinator at the Loyola College for Diversity and Sustainability and Coordinator of the Loyola Sustainability Research Centre.
About the Speakers:
• Donna Kahérakwas Goodleaf is Turtle Clan and is a citizen from the Kanien’kehá:ka (Mohawk) Nation, Kahnawake Territory, which is part of the Rotinonhsión:ni Six Nations Iroquois Confederacy. She is a Kanien’kehá:ka educator and scholar who joined Concordia university in January of 2018 as the new Indigenous Curriculum and Pedagogical Advisor for the Centre for Teaching and Learning. Her current primary role as Director, Decolonizing and Indigenizing Curriculum and Pedagogy is to develop university-wide training for Concordia faculty on decolonizing and Indigenizing their curriculum programs of study in ways that re-center the advancement and integration of Indigenous peoples’ diverse humanities - intellectual, scientific and cultural knowledge systems, worldviews, epistemologies, histories, research and pedagogies across all academic units. She also serves on Concordia University’s Indigenous Directions Leadership Council.
• Rebecca Tittler is a second-generation settler here in Tiohtiá:ke. She first joined Concordia's Loyola College for Diversity and Sustainability in 2013 as an instructor, adding her current position asAcademic Advisor and Administrative Coordinator at the College and Coordinator of the Loyola Sustainability Research Centre in 2016. In both roles, she has worked and continues to work towards the development of sustainability curriculum that incorporates Indigenous expertise and knowledge systems.
